section.title: oosqlSetAuthorizer
section.para: Registers a routine that is called while SQL is prepared, to allow or deny each action the SQL would do.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
rtnName [required]
The name of the public routine to call for each action, or the empty string to remove the routine registered before. See the rules for callback routines.
userData [optional]
Any object, passed to the routine as its sixth argument. If it is omitted, the routine receives .nil.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error.

The routine is called with six arguments: the action, one of the Authorizer Action Code constants, such as SELECT, READ, or DELETE; two strings that depend on the action, such as the name of the table and of the column; the name of the database; the name of the trigger or view that causes the action; and the user data. The strings that do not apply are empty. The routine must return one of the Authorizer Return Code constants: OK to allow the action, IGNORE to ignore it, for a column read it reads NULL, or DENY to make the preparation fail with AUTH (23), not authorized.
The routine is called when the SQL is prepared, not when it is executed. It must not use the connection.
The functionality of the oosqlSetAuthorizer routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_set_authorizer API.
The setAuthorizer method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same with a method of an object; see also authorizerCallBack.

This example forbids deleting rows:
rc = oosqlSetAuthorizer(db, 'noDelete') say oosqlExec(db, "DELETE FROM foods WHERE id = 1;") rows. = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT name FROM foods WHERE id = 1;", .true) say rows.1['NAME'] rc = oosqlSetAuthorizer(db, '') /* Output: SQLite Error: rc = 23, not authorized Bagels */
::routine noDelete public use arg action, arg1, arg2, dbName, trigger if action == .ooSQLite~DELETE then return .ooSQLite~DENY return .ooSQLite~OK

section.title: oosqlSoftHeapLimit64
section.para: Sets or queries the soft limit on the amount of memory that SQLite uses.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
n [required]
The limit, in bytes. A positive number sets the limit, 0 removes it, and a negative number leaves it as it is, to query it.
The limit that was in place before the call, or 0 if there was none.

The limit is soft: when the memory in use approaches it, SQLite frees pages from its cache, but it exceeds the limit rather than fail. The limit applies to the whole process. By default there is no limit.
The functionality of the oosqlSoftHeapLimit64 routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_soft_heap_limit64 API.
The softHeapLimit64 method of the ooSQLite class does the same.

This example sets a limit of 8 megabytes, queries it, and restores the previous one:
old = oosqlSoftHeapLimit64(8 * 1024 * 1024) say 'Limit: ' oosqlSoftHeapLimit64(-1) call oosqlSoftHeapLimit64 old say 'Restored:' oosqlSoftHeapLimit64(-1) /* Output: Limit: 8388608 Restored: 0 */

section.title: oosqlSourceID
section.para: Returns the source identifier of the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.
A string with the date and time of the check-in of the SQLite source code, and its SHA3-256 hash.
The source identifier tells exactly which SQLite source code was built, also between builds of the same version. It is the same as the SOURCE_ID constant when ooSQLite.cls and the library match.
The functionality of the oosqlSourceID routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_sourceid API.
The sourceID method of the ooSQLite class does the same.

This example displays the source identifier:
say oosqlSourceID() /* Output might be: 2026-03-06 16:01:44 557aeb43869d3585137b17690cb3b64f7de6921774daae9e56403c3717dceab6 */

section.title: oosqlSql
section.para: Returns the SQL text of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
The text of the SQL statement, as it was given to oosqlPrepare. When the text given to oosqlPrepare held more than one statement, only the first one is returned, because only that one was prepared.
The text does not change when values are bound to the parameters: the parameters are still shown as they were written.
The functionality of the oosqlSql routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_sql API.
The sql method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example executes, one by one, all the statements in a string. It uses the _tail argument of oosqlPrepare to get what follows each statement, and displays each statement before executing it:
sql = "CREATE TABLE t(a); INSERT INTO t VALUES(1); INSERT INTO t VALUES(2);" do while sql <> '' rc = oosqlPrepare(db, sql~strip, 'stmt', 'sql') if rc <> .ooSQLite~OK then leave if oosqlIsHandleNull(stmt) then leave -- only blanks or comments were left say oosqlSql(stmt) rc = oosqlStep(stmt) call oosqlFinalize stmt end /* Output: CREATE TABLE t(a); INSERT INTO t VALUES(1); INSERT INTO t VALUES(2); */

section.title: oosqlStatus
section.para: Retrieves runtime status information about the performance of SQLite, and optionally resets its highwater mark.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
op [required]
The status parameter to retrieve, one of the Status Parameter constants, such as STATUS_MEMORY_USED.
result [required]
A Stem object, not the name of a stem, in which the values are returned. Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if it is not a Stem object. On success, these tails of the stem are set: CURRENT, the current value of the parameter, and HIGHWATER, its highest recorded value.
reset [optional]
If true, the highwater mark is reset to the current value after it is retrieved. The default is false.
Returns OK on success, or MISUSE if op is not a valid status parameter. On error, the stem is not changed.

The values are for the whole process, not for a database connection: see oosqlDbStatus for those. Some parameters do not record the highest value, and others record only the highest value; for parameters that do not record the highest value, reset is ignored.
The functionality of the oosqlStatus routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_status API.
The status method of the ooSQLite class does the same, with a Directory object instead of a stem.

This example displays how much memory SQLite is using, and how many allocations it has:
rc = oosqlStatus(.ooSQLite~STATUS_MEMORY_USED, s.) if rc == .ooSQLite~OK then say 'Memory used:' s.current 'bytes, highest:' s.highWater 'bytes' rc = oosqlStatus(.ooSQLite~STATUS_MALLOC_COUNT, s.) if rc == .ooSQLite~OK then say 'Allocations:' s.current', highest:' s.highWater /* Output might be: Memory used: 63688 bytes, highest: 63712 bytes Allocations: 136, highest: 137 */

section.title: oosqlStep
section.para: Executes a prepared statement, or advances it to its next result row.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.

One of the Result Code constants. The most common ones are ROW, when a new result row is ready, and its values can be retrieved with the oosqlColumn routines; DONE, when the statement has run to completion: there are no more rows, or, for a statement that returns no data, it has been executed; and BUSY, when the database is locked by another connection, and the statement can be stepped again later, see oosqlBusyTimeOut and oosqlBusyHandler.

Any other code is an error, which oosqlErrMsg describes. ooSQLite enables extended result codes for every connection, so the code is often an extended one, such as CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE (2067) for a duplicate value in a UNIQUE column, rather than CONSTRAINT (19).

A statement that returns data, such as a SELECT, is stepped once for each result row, and once more to get DONE. A statement that returns no data, such as an INSERT, is executed by a single step, which returns DONE on success. After DONE or an error, do not step the statement again before resetting it.
The functionality of the oosqlStep routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_step API.
The step method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example displays all the rows of a query, and checks that it ended without error:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT name FROM foods ORDER BY name;", 'stmt') do forever rc = oosqlStep(stmt) if rc <> .ooSQLite~ROW then leave say oosqlColumnText(stmt, 1) end if rc <> .ooSQLite~DONE then say 'Error' rc':' oosqlErrMsg(db) call oosqlFinalize stmt

section.title: oosqlStmtBusy
section.para: Tests if a prepared statement has been stepped, but has not run to completion and has not been reset.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle can be null.
Returns true if oosqlStep has been invoked at least once, and the statement has neither returned DONE nor been reset. Otherwise, and for a null handle, returns false.
The functionality of the oosqlStmtBusy routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_stmt_busy API.
The stmtBusy method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example shows the value of oosqlStmtBusy, and of oosqlStmtReadonly, while a query is executed:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT name FROM foods;", 'stmt') say oosqlStmtReadonly(stmt) oosqlStmtBusy(stmt) -- 1 0 rc = oosqlStep(stmt) say oosqlStmtBusy(stmt) -- 1 rc = oosqlReset(stmt) say oosqlStmtBusy(stmt) -- 0 call oosqlFinalize stmt

section.title: oosqlStmtReadonly
section.para: Tests if a prepared statement makes no direct changes to the database.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
Returns true if the statement does not write to the database, such as a SELECT, and false if it can, such as an INSERT, an UPDATE, or a DELETE.

A statement can be read only and still change the database indirectly, through a user defined function that executes SQL of its own. Transaction control statements, such as BEGIN and COMMIT, are read only, because they make no changes by themselves.
The functionality of the oosqlStmtReadonly routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_stmt_readonly API.
The stmtReadonly method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.
See the example of oosqlStmtBusy.

section.title: &changed11;oosqlStmtStatus
section.para: Returns the value of one of the performance counters of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
op [required]
The counter to return, one of the Status Parameter (stmt) constants, such as STMTSTATUS_FULLSCAN_STEP or STMTSTATUS_VM_STEP.
reset [optional]
If true, the counter is set to 0 after its value is returned. The default is false.
The value of the counter. For an op that is not one of the constants, 0 is returned, and nothing is reset.
The counters accumulate over all the executions of the statement, also after a reset, until they are reset with the reset argument. They can help find out whether a query would benefit from an index.
The functionality of the oosqlStmtStatus routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_stmt_status API.
The stmtStatus method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example runs a query and displays some of its counters. There is no index on the price column, so the whole table is scanned, and the result has to be sorted:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT name FROM foods WHERE price > 1 ORDER BY name;", 'stmt') do while oosqlStep(stmt) == .ooSQLite~ROW end say 'Full scan steps:' oosqlStmtStatus(stmt, .ooSQLite~STMTSTATUS_FULLSCAN_STEP) say 'Sorts: ' oosqlStmtStatus(stmt, .ooSQLite~STMTSTATUS_SORT) say 'VM steps: ' oosqlStmtStatus(stmt, .ooSQLite~STMTSTATUS_VM_STEP, .true) say 'VM steps now: ' oosqlStmtStatus(stmt, .ooSQLite~STMTSTATUS_VM_STEP) call oosqlFinalize stmt /* Output: Full scan steps: 3 Sorts: 1 VM steps: 47 VM steps now: 0 */

section.title: oosqlStrGlob
section.para: Tests if a string matches a pattern, with the rules of the GLOB operator of SQLite.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
glob [required]
The pattern. * matches any sequence of characters, ? any single character, and [...] any of the characters between the brackets, which can include ranges such as a-z.
str [required]
The string to test.
Returns 0 if the string matches the pattern, and a number that is not 0 if it does not. Note that 0, which is false in Rexx, means a match.
The comparison is case sensitive, as the GLOB operator is: *.txt does not match a.TXT. The return value follows the convention of string comparison functions in C, where 0 means equal.
The functionality of the oosqlStrGlob routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_strglob API.
The strGlob method of the ooSQLite class does the same.

This example displays the names that start with Ba or ba:
do name over .array~of('Bagels', 'Bacon', 'bread', 'Cheese') if oosqlStrGlob('[Bb]a*', name) == 0 then say name end /* Output: Bagels Bacon */

section.title: &changed11;oosqlTableColumnMetadata
section.para: Retrieves metadata about a column of a table of a database connection.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to an open database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
tableName [required]
The name of the table. It must be a table, not a view. The name is case insensitive.
columnName [required]
The name of the column. The name is case insensitive. The names rowid, oid, and _rowid_ are accepted for the rowid of the table.
results [required]
A Stem object, not the name of a stem, in which the metadata are returned. Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if it is not a Stem object. On success, these tails of the stem are set:
DATATYPE
The declared type of the column, or the empty string if the column was declared without a type.
COLLATIONSEQUENCE
The name of the default collation sequence of the column.
NOTNULL
True if the column has a NOT NULL constraint, otherwise false.
PRIMARYKEY
True if the column is part of the primary key, otherwise false.
AUTOINCREMENT
True if the column is AUTOINCREMENT, otherwise false.
dbName [optional]
The name of the database: main, temp, or the name of an attached database. If it is omitted, or is the empty string, all the databases of the connection are searched, in the order SQLite uses for a table name that is not qualified.

Returns OK on success, or ERROR if the table or the column does not exist, or the table is a view; oosqlErrMsg describes the error, for example no such table column: foods.weight. On error, the stem is not changed.

When columnName names the rowid, and the table has a column declared INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, the metadata of that column is returned. When it has none, the metadata is: data type INTEGER, collation sequence BINARY, not null false, primary key true, and auto increment false.

The functionality of the oosqlTableColumnMetadata routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_table_column_metadata API. The order of the arguments is not the same: the optional database name is the last one.
The tableColumnMetadata method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same, with a Directory object instead of a stem.

This example displays the metadata of some columns of the foods table, and then asks for a column that does not exist:
do col over .array~of('id', 'name', 'price', 'rowid') rc = oosqlTableColumnMetadata(db, 'foods', col, m.) if rc == .ooSQLite~OK then say col~left(6) m.dataType~left(8) m.collationSequence - m.notNull m.primaryKey m.autoIncrement end rc = oosqlTableColumnMetadata(db, 'foods', 'weight', m.) say rc oosqlErrMsg(db) /* Output: id INTEGER BINARY 0 1 0 name TEXT BINARY 0 0 0 price REAL BINARY 0 0 0 rowid INTEGER BINARY 0 1 0 1 no such table column: foods.weight */

section.title: oosqlThreadSafe
section.para: Tells whether the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses was built with support for threads.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.

The value of the SQLITE_THREADSAFE compile-time option: 0 if the library was built without support for threads, 1 for the serialized threading mode, 2 for the multi-thread mode. ooSQLite builds SQLite with the value 1, so the routine returns 1.
The value is the default threading mode. The mode can be changed when a connection is opened, with the OPEN_NOMUTEX and OPEN_FULLMUTEX flags of oosqlOpen, but not to or from 0.
The functionality of the oosqlThreadSafe routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_threadsafe API.
The threadSafe method of the ooSQLite class does the same.

This example displays the threading mode:
say 'Threading mode:' oosqlThreadSafe() /* Output: Threading mode: 1 */

section.title: oosqlTotalChanges
section.para: Returns the number of rows changed, inserted, or deleted since a database connection was opened.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
The number of rows.

The count includes the changes made by triggers and by foreign key actions, but not those made to carry out REPLACE constraints, rollbacks, or DROP TABLE. oosqlChanges counts the changes of the last statement only.
The functionality of the oosqlTotalChanges routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_total_changes API.
The totalChanges method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.
See the example of oosqlChanges.

section.title: &changed11;oosqlTrace
section.para: Registers a routine that is called with the text of each SQL statement when it starts executing.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
rtnName [required]
The name of the public routine to call for each statement, or the empty string to remove the routine registered before. See the rules for callback routines.
userData [optional]
Any object, passed to the routine as its second argument. If it is omitted, the routine receives .nil.
Returns the userData of the routine that was registered before, or .nil if there was none, or it had no user data.

The routine is called with two arguments: the SQL text, and the user data. When a trigger starts, it is also called, with a comment that names the trigger as the SQL text. It must return a whole number, which is ignored.
A connection has only one of trace and profile routine: registering one removes the other.
The functionality of the oosqlTrace routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_trace API.
The trace method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same with a method of an object; see also traceCallBack.

This example displays each statement executed by a call to oosqlExec, with a prefix given as the user data:
rc = oosqlTrace(db, 'showSql', 'SQL>') rc = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT count(*) FROM foods; UPDATE foods SET price = 3 WHERE id = 1;") rc = oosqlTrace(db, '') /* Output: SQL> SELECT count(*) FROM foods; SQL> UPDATE foods SET price = 3 WHERE id = 1; */
::routine showSql public use arg sql, prefix say prefix sql return 0

section.title: oosqlUpdateHook
section.para: Registers a routine that is called whenever a row is inserted, updated, or deleted.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
rtnName [required]
The name of the public routine to call for each row changed, or the empty string to remove the routine registered before. See the rules for callback routines.
userData [optional]
Any object, passed to the routine as its fifth argument. If it is omitted, the routine receives .nil.
Returns the userData of the routine that was registered before, or .nil if there was none, or it had no user data.

The routine is called with five arguments: the operation, which is one of the Authorizer Action Code constants INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE; the name of the database, such as main; the name of the table; the rowid of the row, after the change for an update; and the user data. It must return a whole number, which is ignored.

The routine is not called for changes to tables without a rowid, to internal tables, or for the rows deleted by a DELETE without a WHERE clause, which SQLite carries out by truncating the table. It must not use the connection: it must not prepare or execute SQL on it.
The functionality of the oosqlUpdateHook routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_update_hook API.
The updateHook method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same with a method of an object; see also updateHookCallBack.

This example displays the rows changed by an UPDATE and a DELETE:
rc = oosqlUpdateHook(db, 'showChange') rc = oosqlExec(db, "UPDATE foods SET price = 2 WHERE type_id = 1; DELETE FROM foods WHERE id = 3;") rc = oosqlUpdateHook(db, '') /* Output: UPDATE main.foods rowid 1 UPDATE main.foods rowid 2 DELETE main.foods rowid 3 */
::routine showChange public use arg op, dbName, tableName, rowid select when op == .ooSQLite~INSERT then what = 'INSERT' when op == .ooSQLite~UPDATE then what = 'UPDATE' otherwise what = 'DELETE' end say what dbName'.'tableName 'rowid' rowid return 0

section.title: &changed11;oosqlValueBlob
section.para: Returns one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function as a blob.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the routine: the fourth and following arguments of the routine of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob.

A string with the bytes of the value, including any NUL characters. A value that is not a blob is converted: text is returned as is, and a number as its text representation. An empty blob returns the empty string, and a NULL value returns the .nil object.

What is said here applies to all the oosqlValue routines. They are used inside the routines of the functions and aggregates defined with oosqlCreateFunction. SQLite passes each argument of the SQL function to the routine as a Pointer object, the sqlValue: the fourth and following arguments of the routine of a function, and the fifth and following arguments of the step routine of an aggregate. The oosqlValue routines return the value in the form that is asked for, converting it if needed. oosqlValueType tells which type the value has.

A sqlValue is only valid during the invocation of the routine that received it. &changed11;A Pointer that is not a value, or a value that is no longer valid, raises a syntax error, 88.900: see Handles. Before ooSQLite 1.1 it could crash the interpreter.
oosqlValueInt, oosqlValueInt64, oosqlValueDouble, oosqlValueText, and oosqlValueBlob return .nil for a NULL value. Use oosqlValueType to test for NULL before asking for the value.
The functionality of the oosqlValueBlob routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_blob API.
The blob method of the ooSQLValue class does the same in the object orientated interface.
Before ooSQLite 1.1, this routine returned a Pointer to the data, which was only useful to pass it, with its size, to oosqlResultBlob, and .nil for both an empty blob and NULL.

This example defines a describe function that tells an empty blob from NULL, and displays the bytes of any other value:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "describe", 1, "describeRtn") sql = "SELECT describe(x'CAFE'), describe(x''), describe(NULL)," - "describe('ab');" rows = oosqlExec(db, sql, .true, .ooSQLite~OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS) say rows[2]~toString('l', ' / ') /* Output: 2 byte(s): CAFE / empty / NULL / 2 byte(s): 6162 */
::routine describeRtn public use arg db, context, userData, value data = oosqlValueBlob(value) select when data == .nil then text = 'NULL' when data == '' then text = 'empty' otherwise text = oosqlValueBytes(value) 'byte(s):' data~c2x end call oosqlResultText context, text return 0

section.title: oosqlValueBytes
section.para: Returns the size in bytes of one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the routine: the fourth and following arguments of the routine of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob.
The size of a blob, or of the UTF-8 text of any other value: the number 3.9 has 3 bytes. A NULL value has 0 bytes.

The size is that of the value as it is when the routine is invoked: oosqlValueNumericType can convert a text to a number, and then its size changes. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the oosqlValueBytes routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_bytes API.
The bytes method of the ooSQLValue class does the same in the object orientated interface.
See the example of oosqlValueBlob.

section.title: &changed11;oosqlValueDouble
section.para: Returns one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function as a floating point number.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the routine: the fourth and following arguments of the routine of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob.

The value as a number, with all its precision: the shortest number, of up to 17 significant digits, that is converted back to the same floating point value. Text that starts with a number is converted to that number; a blob, and text that does not start with a number, return 0. For a NULL value, the .nil object is returned.

A Rexx program computes with 9 digits unless it sets NUMERIC DIGITS: the number keeps its precision, but an arithmetic operation on it is rounded to the current setting. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the oosqlValueDouble routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_double API.
The double method of the ooSQLValue class does the same in the object orientated interface.
Before ooSQLite 1.1, the number was returned with 9 significant digits only: 3.141592653589793 was returned as 3.14159265.

This example defines a function that returns, as text, the number that the Rexx routine receives:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "asSeenByRexx", 1, "asSeenByRexxRtn") sql = "SELECT asSeenByRexx(pi()), asSeenByRexx(0.1), asSeenByRexx('2.50');" rows = oosqlExec(db, sql, .true, .ooSQLite~OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS) say rows[2]~toString('l', ' ') /* Output: 3.141592653589793 0.1 2.5 */
::routine asSeenByRexxRtn public use arg db, context, userData, value call oosqlResultText context, oosqlValueDouble(value) return 0

section.title: oosqlValueInt
section.para: Returns one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function as a 32-bit integer.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the routine: the fourth and following arguments of the routine of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob.

The value as a whole number. A floating point value is truncated, so 3.9 is 3, and text that starts with a number is converted to that number; a blob, and text that does not start with a number, return 0. For a NULL value, the .nil object is returned.

When the value does not fit in 32 bits, only its lower 32 bits are returned, and the result is not meaningful: use oosqlValueInt64 for values that can be that large. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the oosqlValueInt routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_int API.
The int method of the ooSQLValue class does the same in the object orientated interface.
See the examples of oosqlResultInt64 and oosqlResultZeroBlob.

section.title: &added11;oosqlValueInt64
section.para: Returns one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function as a 64-bit integer.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the routine: the fourth and following arguments of the routine of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob.
The value as a whole number, converted as oosqlValueInt does. For a NULL value, the .nil object is returned.

The routine that computes with the value may need a higher NUMERIC DIGITS setting than the default of 9, as the example does. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the oosqlValueInt64 routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_int64 API.
The int64 method of the ooSQLValue class does the same in the object orientated interface.
This routine is new in ooSQLite 1.1. Before, the classic interface could not read an argument that does not fit in 32 bits as a whole number.

This example defines a half function, which works with numbers that do not fit in 32 bits:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "half", 1, "halfRtn") sql = "SELECT half(9000000000) AS a, half(7) AS b, half('41') AS c," - "quote(half(NULL)) AS d;" rows = oosqlExec(db, sql, .true, .ooSQLite~OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS) say rows[2]~toString('l', ' ') /* Output: 4500000000 3 20 NULL */
::routine halfRtn public use arg db, context, userData, value numeric digits 19 n = oosqlValueInt64(value) if n == .nil then call oosqlResultNull context else call oosqlResultInt64 context, n % 2 return 0

section.title: oosqlValueNumericType
section.para: Returns the datatype of one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function, after converting a text that looks like a number to that number.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the routine: the fourth and following arguments of the routine of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob.
One of the Fundamental Datatype constants, as oosqlValueType returns. For a text that is a well formed number, possibly with spaces around it, the type is INTEGER or FLOAT instead of TEXT.

The conversion is done in place: once this routine has converted a text, the value is that number, for oosqlValueType, oosqlValueText, oosqlValueBytes, and the other routines. Use oosqlValueType first when the original type matters. A text that only starts with a number, such as '12abc', is not converted. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the oosqlValueNumericType routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_numeric_type API.
The numericType method of the ooSQLValue class does the same in the object orientated interface.

This example displays, for some texts, the type before the conversion, the type that oosqlValueNumericType returns, and the type after it:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "kinds", 1, "kindsRtn") sql = "SELECT kinds('12'), kinds(' 3.5 '), kinds('12abc');" rows = oosqlExec(db, sql, .true, .ooSQLite~OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS) say rows[2]~toString('l', ' / ') /* Output: TEXT INTEGER INTEGER / TEXT FLOAT FLOAT / TEXT TEXT TEXT */
::routine kindsRtn public use arg db, context, userData, value names = .array~of('INTEGER', 'FLOAT', 'TEXT', 'BLOB', 'NULL') before = names[oosqlValueType(value)] numeric = names[oosqlValueNumericType(value)] after = names[oosqlValueType(value)] call oosqlResultText context, before numeric after return 0

section.title: oosqlValueText
section.para: Returns one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function as a string.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the routine: the fourth and following arguments of the routine of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob.

The value as a string: text as is, and a number as its text representation. For a blob, the bytes before its first NUL character are returned: use oosqlValueBlob for all of them. For a NULL value, the .nil object is returned.

This is the routine used most to read the arguments of a function, because any value can be represented as a string. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the oosqlValueText routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_text API.
The text method of the ooSQLValue class does the same in the object orientated interface.
See the examples of oosqlResultText and oosqlResultInt.

section.title: oosqlValueType
section.para: Returns the datatype of one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the routine: the fourth and following arguments of the routine of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob.
One of the Fundamental Datatype constants: INTEGER, FLOAT, TEXT, BLOB, or SQLNULL.

SQLite is dynamically typed: the same function can get values of different types in different invocations, whatever the declared types of the columns they come from. oosqlValueNumericType also tells whether a text looks like a number. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the oosqlValueType routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_type API.
The type method of the ooSQLValue class does the same in the object orientated interface.

This example defines a kind function that returns the name of the type of its argument:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "kind", 1, "kindRtn") sql = "SELECT kind(12), kind(1.5), kind('12'), kind(x'00'), kind(NULL);" rows = oosqlExec(db, sql, .true, .ooSQLite~OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS) say rows[2]~toString('l', ' ') /* Output: INTEGER FLOAT TEXT BLOB NULL */
::routine kindRtn public use arg db, context, userData, value names = .array~of('INTEGER', 'FLOAT', 'TEXT', 'BLOB', 'NULL') call oosqlResultText context, names[oosqlValueType(value)] return 0

section.title: oosqlVersion
section.para: Returns the version of the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses, from the version string of the SQLite code.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.
The version, such as 3.52.0, the same string that oosqlLibVersion returns.
This routine exists for completeness: it is the same as oosqlLibVersion. It does not return the version of ooSQLite; ooSQLiteVersion does.
The value returned is that of the sqlite3_version string constant of the SQLite code.
The sqlite3Version method of the ooSQLite class does the same. The version method of that class does something else: it returns the version of ooSQLite, as ooSQLiteVersion does.

This example shows that the two routines return the same string:
say oosqlVersion() (oosqlVersion() == oosqlLibVersion()) /* Output might be: 3.52.0 1 */
